newsitem.title: USA: New funding methods needed for gold mining - Morgan.
newsitem.headline: New funding methods needed for gold mining - Morgan.

text.p: A surge in gold exploration spending in the 1990s is forcing increasing use of new funding techniques such as asset-backed securitization and commodity-linked financing said J.P. Morgan vice president for commodities Kevin Crisp.

"Increasingly, traditional sources of funding -- balance sheet, equity, project finance and syndication -- may become inadequate because of the magnitude of demand," Crisp told the annual conference of Gold and Silver Institute.

Worldwide non-ferrous metals exploration spending rose 30 percent to $4.6 billion in 1996 and was more than double the amount spent in 1992, he said. About 61 percent of the total spending was directed toward finding gold reserves.
"Adding to the demand for funding in the future will be a spate of privatizations of state mining assets," Crisp said.
In 1997, such privatizations will probably include CVG in Venezuela, CVRD in Brazil, Polish copper producer KGHM and Zambian copper producer ZCCM, he said.
In 1998 alone, about 25 new gold mines are expected to come on stream, with a combined life-of-mine-production rate of 140 tonnes annually.

About 50 percent of the funding for these sorts of projects will come from gold mining company cash flow, as in recent years gold miners have reinvested about $40 for every ounce of gold produced, Crisp said.
But "a resurgence in gold loan activity remains a distinct possibility as companies move away from conventional project financing," Crisp said.

Forward hedging may also continue to provide funds for some companies, as active hedgers such as Barrick Gold and Ashanti Goldfields have received prices for their metal sales well in excess of prevailing spot rates in recent years, he said.

Equity markets have also funded high-risk exploration, acquisitions, and new mine development, but "it is not clear that this still highly specialized market is deep enough to support the levels of funding that are now being contemplated," Crisp said.
"The key goal is to get new investor groups who are natural lenders for longer term projects into the market," he said.
Structured financing, combining equity issues, bank funding, forward sales and currency hedges, can be used to improve credit quality and attract new investors, he said.

A recent example was the funding program for JCI Ltd's Western Areas South Deep section in South Africa which included a rights offering, supported by a mix of forward sales, rand- gold call options and rand-dollar call options, he said.
But techniques such as asset-backed securitization or commodity-linked finance may also be used.
In a generic asset-backed securitization, a producer creates a long term export contract with a bank and both parties assign the contract rights to an offshore trust.
The trust in turn issues notes to investors which are amortized by either deliveries of the commodity or export payments generated under the contract.

But the notes may be attractive to investors because the structure means the notes have a very strong chance of being rated as investment grade, Crisp said. ((--Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1640))
